title: Dock workers at Rotterdam terminal vote to extend strike by 48 hours
summary: Dock workers at a large container terminal in Rotterdam voted to extend their strike by two more days, leaving about 60 ships waiting offshore. The union says talks on night-shift pay broke down on Sunday evening.
body_html:
ROTTERDAM, 27 October (Meridian) - dock workers at a large container terminal in Rotterdam voted on Monday to extend their strike by 48 hours, deepening delays at one of Europe's busiest ports.

The Harbour Workers' Federation said 1,150 members backed the extension in a show of hands at a union hall near the Maas river, with about 40 voting against. The walkout began on Friday over night-shift pay and rest periods.

Port authority figures seen by Meridian show about 60 container ships are anchored or slowly circling offshore, up from 38 on Saturday. The authority said the average wait for a berth has risen to 71 hours. The strike is the longest at the terminal since 2019. Retailers have warned that Christmas stock, much of it shipped from Asia in the past three weeks, could reach shelves late if the dispute drags into December, and two car makers said they are watching parts deliveries closely.

"Our members are not asking for the moon," said Anneke Dijkhof, the federation's lead negotiator. "They are asking not to work 12-hour nights with a 6-hour gap before the next shift. Management walked away from the table on Sunday evening."

The terminal operator, Delta Gate Terminals, said it had offered a 4.5 percent pay rise and a pilot scheme for shorter rotations at two of its six quays. A company spokesperson, Joris van Rensen, said the offer was "generous and final in its current form" but that the firm remained ready to meet again.

Freight forwarders are already rerouting some cargo through Antwerp and Hamburg. The Northern Shippers' Council estimated the stoppage is costing the supply chain about 30 million euros a day in delays and storage fees. The Dutch labour ministry said a mediator will be offered to both sides on Tuesday. No new talks are scheduled.

title: Coastal states open Quebec City talks on shared rules for Arctic shipping
summary: Delegates from eight coastal states opened three days of talks in Quebec City on common safety and emissions rules for ships using Arctic routes. Environment groups want a ban on heavy fuel oil north of the Arctic Circle.
body_html:
QUEBEC CITY, 27 October (Meridian) - delegates from eight coastal states opened three days of talks in Quebec City on Monday aimed at agreeing common safety and emissions rules for ships using Arctic sea routes.

The Northern Waters Forum, a body set up four years ago by the participating governments, says commercial traffic in the region has risen by about 35 percent since 2022 as summer ice retreats. It counted 1,420 voyages through the main northern passages this season.

The draft text on the table would require ice-capable hulls for all vessels above 5,000 tonnes, a joint search-and-rescue plan, and a phase-out of heavy fuel oil by 2031. Several delegations said the fuel provision is the hardest to settle. Observers said the talks are the first in which all eight governments have sent ministers rather than officials. Canada and the Nordic states are pushing for binding rules, while two delegations prefer voluntary guidance, and a compromise is likely to combine mandatory safety standards with softer emissions language.

"We are all asking the same question: what happens when a fully loaded vessel gets into trouble 900 kilometres from the nearest port?" said Mireille Tessier, who chairs the forum's technical committee. "Without common rules the answer is that nobody is ready."

Environment groups gathered outside the conference centre, calling for an outright ban on heavy fuel oil north of the Arctic Circle. The Polar Seas Alliance, a campaign coalition, said burning the fuel in the region releases black carbon that speeds up melting.

Shipping lobbyists argue that a short deadline would raise freight costs on routes that already compete with the Suez Canal. A spokesman for the Association of Northern Carriers, Henrik Lund, said operators accept the safety package but want a longer transition on fuel. A final communique is expected on Wednesday. Any agreement would still need approval by each government.

title: Floods displace 40,000 people in northern Mozambique, aid agencies say
summary: Heavy rain has pushed rivers over their banks in northern Mozambique, displacing about 40,000 people. Relief agencies say roads are cut and they are flying in tents and clean water.
body_html:
MAPUTO, 26 October (Meridian) - floods caused by a week of heavy rain have displaced about 40,000 people in northern Mozambique, aid agencies said on Sunday, and rivers are still rising in two provinces.

The Southern Relief Network, a coalition of 14 charities, said the worst-hit districts are along the Lugenda and Montepuez rivers, where entire villages have been cut off. Its field coordinator, Amina Chitsulo, said at least nine people have died and 22 are missing.

Local authorities have opened 31 temporary shelters in schools and churches. Many hold two or three times their intended numbers, and aid workers report shortages of clean water and mosquito nets. The flooding is the worst in the region in six years. In 2020 a similar event displaced about 25,000 people, and officials say the larger number this time reflects new settlements built on low-lying ground along the river banks, where many families have no savings to fall back on.

"People are sleeping on classroom floors with no blankets," Chitsulo said by telephone. "The next priority is clean water. We have seen the first cases of watery diarrhoea in two camps."

The national disaster management office said the main northern road is under water in three places, and that helicopters and boats are the only way to reach some areas. It has asked for about 12 million dollars to cover the next 60 days.

Meteorologists at the regional weather service said more rain is expected on Tuesday and Wednesday, though lighter than last week. The rainy season normally runs until March, and forecasters have warned that this year's is likely to be wetter than average. Two charities have started airlifting tents, tarpaulins and water purification tablets from Nacala.

title: Magnitude 6.1 earthquake strikes off Sumatra coast, no tsunami warning issued
summary: A magnitude 6.1 earthquake struck off the coast of Sumatra on Tuesday, shaking buildings in coastal towns. Officials said no tsunami warning was issued and there were no immediate reports of deaths.
body_html:
JAKARTA, 27 October (Meridian) - a magnitude 6.1 earthquake struck off the western coast of Sumatra on Tuesday, shaking buildings in coastal towns and sending residents into the streets, officials said.

The Pacific Rim Seismology Centre, a monitoring group, said the quake hit at 08:42 local time at a depth of 38 kilometres, about 70 kilometres from the nearest coastline. It recorded four aftershocks of magnitude 4.0 or more within two hours.

Local disaster officials said no tsunami warning was issued because the quake was too small and too deep to cause a significant wave. Sea levels at three nearby gauges were normal. A fishing community on the nearest island reported that boats returned to harbour as a precaution, and the local port authority briefly stopped ferry services. By midday the services had resumed, though passengers were asked to carry life jackets and to avoid the lower decks until inspections were complete.

"We have no reports of deaths so far," said Rina Hakim, a spokeswoman for the provincial disaster agency. "Teams are checking schools, health clinics and bridges. We ask residents to stay away from damaged buildings."

Residents of Padang described furniture sliding across floors and cracks appearing in plaster walls. Power was cut for about an hour in two districts, and mobile networks were patchy.

Sumatra lies on the Pacific Ring of Fire and is regularly hit by earthquakes. Officials said they will publish a first damage count by evening. This story is being updated. Indonesia's national disaster agency said it has put rescue teams and mobile hospitals on standby in the province, and that it will brief reporters again at 15:00 local time.

title: Health ministers agree to pool vaccine stockpiles in Geneva deal
summary: Health ministers from 31 countries agreed in Geneva to pool part of their vaccine stockpiles for use in outbreaks. The scheme is due to start in January and cover six diseases.
body_html:
GENEVA, 27 October (Meridian) - health ministers from 31 countries agreed on Monday to pool part of their emergency vaccine stockpiles so doses can be released quickly to countries facing outbreaks.

Under the Global Health Compact, signed after two days of talks in Geneva, each member will set aside 5 percent of its stockpile for a shared reserve. The scheme is due to start in January and will cover six diseases, including cholera and yellow fever.

A secretariat of 12 staff will decide on releases within 48 hours of a request. Officials said the current process, which relies on bilateral deals, takes an average of 19 days. Delegates said the talks were helped by the experience of recent regional outbreaks, when countries with surplus doses and countries with urgent needs struggled to find each other. The compact includes a clause barring members from imposing export bans on doses assigned to the shared reserve.

"A vaccine that sits in a freezer in one country while an outbreak spreads in another helps no one," said Dr Selma Arvidsson, the Swedish-born chair of the talks. "This is about speed."

The reserve is expected to hold about 14 million doses at launch. A funding gap remains: the compact's budget of 90 million dollars is covered only to 60 percent, according to a draft annex seen by Meridian.

Three countries signed with reservations on how doses would be priced when sold on to non-members. Campaign groups welcomed the deal but said smaller countries need a guaranteed seat on the release committee. Ratification by national parliaments is expected to take until the end of the year.

title: Berlin coalition partners agree compromise on pension reform bill
summary: The three parties in Germany's governing coalition agreed a compromise on a pension reform bill after a late-night meeting. The text keeps the retirement age fixed until 2032 and raises contributions by 0.4 points.
body_html:
BERLIN, 27 October (Meridian) - the three parties of the governing coalition reached a compromise on a pension reform bill after a late-night meeting, party officials said on Monday, clearing the way for a first reading in parliament next week.

The agreement keeps the statutory retirement age fixed until 2032 and raises the contribution rate by 0.4 percentage points, to be shared equally between employers and employees. A proposed cut in the benefit level was dropped.

The deal ends three weeks of public disagreement. The Social Union, the smaller partner, had demanded a guarantee on benefit levels, while the Liberal Alliance wanted a cap on contributions. The compromise includes a review clause in 2030 that lets either side reopen the contribution rate. Pensions have dominated domestic politics since the summer, when a government commission warned that the system would need an extra 40 billion euros a year by 2040 without changes. Opinion polls show about two-thirds of voters want the retirement age left alone, which made that point the hardest for the coalition to concede.

"Nobody got everything they wanted, which is how coalitions are supposed to work," said Katrin Wendt, parliamentary manager of the Social Union group, after the meeting. "But pensioners and workers now have clarity."

The finance ministry estimates the package will cost the federal budget about 3.2 billion euros a year from 2028. A ministry spokesman said the figure is covered in the medium-term plan.

The opposition Conservative Forum called the compromise "a patch, not a reform". Its pensions spokesman, Dieter Lamprecht, said the review clause leaves the real decisions to the next government. The bill needs a simple majority in the lower house, where the coalition holds 41 seats more than the opposition. A vote is pencilled in for late November.

title: French Senate committee backs stricter rules on party donations
summary: A French Senate committee voted to lower the annual cap on donations to political parties and to ban cash gifts above 150 euros. The full Senate will debate the text next month.
body_html:
PARIS, 26 October (Meridian) - a committee of the French Senate voted on Sunday to lower the annual cap on donations to political parties and to ban cash gifts above 150 euros, sending the bill to a full Senate debate next month.

The law and institutions committee approved the text by 22 votes to 11. It would cut the yearly limit per donor from 7,500 euros to 5,000 euros and require parties to publish the names of all donors above 1,000 euros within 30 days.

The bill's rapporteur, Senator Bernard Laval, said recent audits showed that about 9 percent of party funding in the last election cycle came from sources that could not be traced. "Transparency is not a favour to the public, it is a condition of trust," he told reporters. The proposal follows a report by the national audit body last spring that criticised weak checks on cash donations. It also found that some local branches of parties did not file accounts at all, and recommended that the oversight commission be given powers to impose fines of up to 5 percent of a party's annual income.

Parties on the right argued that tighter limits would favour established groups with large membership fees over new movements. Senator Odile Marchetti said the cash ban "punishes volunteers who pass a hat round at local meetings".

The government has not said whether it will back the text. A justice ministry official told Meridian the ministry wants to see an impact study on small parties first.

If the Senate passes the bill, it must still go to the National Assembly, where a similar proposal stalled last year. Campaign finance watchers said the committee's vote was a sign that cross-party support for reform is growing.

title: Valencia regional parliament passes 2027 budget after overnight session
summary: The regional parliament in Valencia approved a 2027 budget of 31.4 billion euros after an overnight session. The plan raises health spending by 6 percent and freezes regional taxes.
body_html:
VALENCIA, 25 October (Meridian) - the regional parliament in Valencia approved a 2027 budget of 31.4 billion euros early on Saturday after a session that lasted more than 14 hours.

The plan passed by 56 votes to 43. It raises health spending by 6 percent, adds 1,200 teaching posts and freezes regional tax rates for a third year.

Regional finance councillor Marta Quesada said the budget assumes growth of 2.1 percent and a deficit of 0.3 percent of regional output. "This is a prudent budget for uncertain times," she said before the vote. The session was longer than expected because the opposition tabled 210 amendments, of which 14 were adopted. Several of those concern the regional audit office, which will receive extra staff to check spending on the new ports zone, a condition that the governing party accepted late on Friday.

The opposition criticised a 480 million euro line for the regional ports and logistics zone, which it called optimistic. Opposition leader Joaquim Ferrer said the money would be better spent on public transport and on repairs to schools damaged in last year's storms.

A small regional party secured an extra 55 million euros for rural broadband in exchange for its votes. Its spokeswoman, Clara Benavent, said the party had "turned a promise into a line in the budget".

Business groups gave a cautious welcome. The Valencia Chamber of Commerce said the tax freeze was positive but warned that delays in paying suppliers remain a problem for small firms. The budget takes effect on 1 January. Spending will be monitored quarterly by the regional audit office, which will publish a report each April.

title: Canadian opposition demands inquiry into federal procurement contracts
summary: Opposition parties in Canada called for a public inquiry after an audit found that a quarter of sampled federal IT contracts were awarded without competition. The government says the findings are being reviewed.
body_html:
OTTAWA, 27 October (Meridian) - opposition parties in Canada demanded a public inquiry on Monday after an audit found that a quarter of a sample of federal technology contracts were awarded without competition.

The report by the auditor's office reviewed 160 contracts worth a combined 2.4 billion Canadian dollars signed over three years. It found 41 had been awarded to a single bidder with no public tender and that in 12 cases the winning price was above the department's own estimate.

At a news conference on Parliament Hill, the Democratic Reform party's procurement critic, Pauline Gagnon, said: "Taxpayers deserve to know who decided, and why. This cannot be left to the departments that made the decisions." The audit also noted that the share of single-bidder contracts rose each year over the period, from 18 percent in the first year to 31 percent in the third. Officials told the auditors that urgent requirements during the pandemic had justified quick awards, an argument the auditors described as no longer convincing.

A spokesperson for the public services minister said the government accepts the audit's recommendations and has already tightened rules on sole-source awards above 100,000 dollars. The spokesperson said an inquiry was "not necessary at this time".

Two of the largest contracts went to Northbridge Systems, an Ottawa software firm. The company said all its contracts followed the rules in force at the time and that it will cooperate with any review.

The public accounts committee is due to take evidence from senior officials on Thursday. Details of the contracts and the audit methodology are still being checked.

title: Brazilian Senate delays vote on rural land bill until next month
summary: The Brazilian Senate postponed a vote on a bill that would ease rules for clearing private rural land. Supporters of the bill say they lack the votes this week.
body_html:
BRASILIA, 27 October (Meridian) - the Brazilian Senate postponed on Monday a vote on a bill that would ease rules for clearing private rural land, after supporters said they did not have enough votes to pass it this week.

The bill would cut the share of a rural property that owners must keep as native vegetation in some regions, from 35 percent to 20 percent. It passed the lower house in September by 276 votes to 190.

Senate leaders said the vote will now take place in the first week of December. Senator Helena Barros, who leads the farm caucus, said talks with undecided members needed "a few more weeks and a few more amendments". The bill's backers say it would let farmers on the agricultural frontier use land that has been idle for years. Critics note that satellite data already show clearing at a record pace in two states, and the debate is being closely watched by buyers of Brazilian beef and soybeans in Europe and Asia.

Environment groups said the delay was a small victory. The Rainforest Watch Institute estimates that the change could open up to 14 million hectares to clearing within a decade, a figure the farm caucus disputes.

"The vote was delayed because senators heard from their own voters," said Institute researcher Tiago Moreira. "There is real concern about water supplies and about the country's climate targets."

Farm groups argue that the current rules make small and mid-sized producers uncompetitive. The National Growers' Federation said the bill would bring legal certainty for 200,000 properties. The government has not taken a formal position, but officials said the environment ministry has asked for safeguards in protected river basins.

title: Wall Street ends higher as chip makers lead rebound
summary: US stocks closed higher on Monday, led by semiconductor makers after a strong earnings report from Halvern Semiconductor. The broad market index gained 1.2 percent.
body_html:
NEW YORK, 27 October (Meridian) - US stocks closed higher on Monday, led by semiconductor makers, as investors bought back into technology shares after last week's sell-off.

The broad market index rose 1.2 percent to close at 6,184 points, while the technology-heavy index gained 1.9 percent. Of the 11 sectors, only utilities ended lower. About 11.4 billion shares changed hands, above the 20-day average.

Halvern Semiconductor jumped 8.7 percent after it raised its fourth-quarter revenue forecast to 5.9 billion dollars, citing demand for data-centre processors. Its supplier, Quillon Materials, gained 5.1 percent. Trading was broad-based, with advancing shares outnumbering decliners by almost three to one on the main exchange. Volatility, as measured by the market's fear gauge, fell to its lowest level in three weeks, and small-cap shares also had a good session, adding 1.6 percent as lending stocks recovered.

"The market was oversold, and Halvern gave people a reason to come back," said Priya Raman, chief strategist at the New York advisory firm Lakeshore Capital. "The question is whether the next batch of earnings can sustain it."

Bond yields eased, with the benchmark 10-year Treasury yield at 4.21 percent from 4.26 percent on Friday. Traders now price in a 62 percent chance of an interest rate cut at the December meeting, according to futures data.

Energy shares were mixed. Falling crude prices weighed on producers while airlines rose, with Skyreach Air up 3.4 percent. Investors will watch retail sales data and a series of earnings reports from consumer companies later this week. The Treasury is due to auction 58 billion dollars of three-year notes on Tuesday, and investors will look for signs of demand after a weak auction last month.

title: Eurozone factory activity shrinks for third month, survey shows
summary: Factory activity in the euro area contracted for a third straight month in October, a business survey showed. Weak orders from Germany and Italy outweighed a small rise in Spain.
body_html:
FRANKFURT, 26 October (Meridian) - factory activity in the euro area contracted for a third straight month in October, a business survey showed on Sunday, with weak orders from Germany and Italy outweighing a small rise in Spain.

The Continental Purchasing Managers' Index for manufacturing came in at 47.8, up slightly from 47.3 in September but still below the 50 mark that separates growth from contraction. Economists polled by Meridian had expected 47.5.

New orders fell for the 14th month in a row and export orders dropped at the fastest pace since spring. Firms reported cutting jobs for the fifth month, though the pace of cuts eased. The figures add to evidence that the region's recovery is uneven. Services activity, covered in a separate survey due on Tuesday, has been holding up better, and economists say the question is whether services strength can offset a manufacturing slump that has now lasted longer than the one in 2023.

"There is no sign of a turn yet," said Lukas Hartmann, an economist at the Frankfurt research house Rhine Analytics. "The small improvement is mostly from suppliers delivering faster, not from stronger demand."

Price pressures were subdued. Input costs fell for the second month and firms said they are passing some savings on to customers, which could help the central bank's effort to bring inflation back to target.

Spain was the bright spot, with its index rising to 50.6, helped by car and food production. Germany's index stood at 45.9 and Italy's at 46.8. The survey, based on replies from about 3,000 manufacturers, was compiled in the first three weeks of the month.

title: Oil slips as inventories build and demand outlook softens
summary: Oil prices fell more than 2 percent on Friday after industry data showed a larger-than-expected build in stockpiles. Forecasters trimmed estimates for next year's demand growth.
body_html:
LONDON, 26 October (Meridian) - oil prices fell more than 2 percent on Friday, heading for a second weekly loss, after industry data showed a larger-than-expected build in stockpiles and forecasters trimmed estimates for next year's demand.

The benchmark North Sea crude contract fell 1.82 dollars to settle at 78.40 dollars a barrel, while the main US contract lost 1.95 dollars to 74.10 dollars. Both are down about 4 percent on the week.

The Energy Data Bureau said commercial crude stocks in the United States rose by 5.3 million barrels last week, against a forecast increase of 1.1 million. Gasoline stocks also rose, a sign that demand is soft ahead of winter. The price decline came despite some supportive news. A cold snap in northern Europe is expected to lift heating oil demand, and a pipeline outage in Libya cut about 90,000 barrels a day, but traders said such factors are small compared with the larger stockpile build and the cautious outlook for growth.

Separately, the Global Energy Outlook group cut its 2027 demand growth forecast to 1.0 million barrels per day from 1.3 million, citing slower industrial activity in Europe and weaker diesel use.

"The market is carrying more oil than it needs, and nobody wants to be the first to blink," said Ingrid Solheim, a senior analyst at the London consultancy Brent Quay Advisory.

Producers' groups are expected to meet next month to discuss output, and traders said talk of a deeper cut had faded after several members publicly said the current level is appropriate. Analysts said the price could find support near 75 dollars, where short-term buyers have stepped in twice this quarter.

title: Shipping group Norvald Lines posts 18 percent drop in quarterly profit
summary: Norvald Lines, a Norwegian container shipping group, reported an 18 percent fall in third-quarter profit as freight rates eased. The company kept its full-year guidance.
body_html:
OSLO, 27 October (Meridian) - Norvald Lines, a Norwegian container shipping group, reported an 18 percent fall in third-quarter operating profit on Monday as freight rates eased and costs for port fees rose.

Operating profit came in at 412 million dollars, against 502 million a year earlier and a mean analyst forecast of 395 million. Revenue slipped 6 percent to 2.9 billion dollars. Shares rose 2.3 percent in early trade in Oslo.

The average rate per container fell 11 percent from the same quarter last year, while volumes carried grew 4 percent. The company said strikes and congestion at European ports had cost it about 35 million dollars in delays. Norvald has cut the number of ports of call on its Asia-Europe routes from 38 to 31 this year to save fuel, and says the reduction has not hurt delivery times. Its two largest customers, both retail groups, renewed their annual contracts in September at lower rates than the year before, according to people familiar with the talks.

"We delivered a decent quarter in a market that is returning to normal," chief executive Sigrun Aasen said in a statement. "We expect the second half to look similar to the third quarter, which is why we are not changing our guidance."

Norvald kept its full-year operating profit forecast of 1.5 billion to 1.8 billion dollars. It also said it will take delivery of four new low-emission vessels in the first quarter, part of a 1.1 billion dollar fleet renewal.

Analysts at the Oslo broker Fjordline Securities said the result showed the group's cost control but that earnings would remain exposed to freight rates. The board proposed an interim dividend of 1.20 Norwegian crowns per share.

title: Alpine Credit Authority keeps rates at 1.75 percent and signals long pause
summary: The Alpine Credit Authority held its main interest rate at 1.75 percent and said it expects no change before spring. The franc weakened slightly after the decision.
body_html:
ZURICH, 27 October (Meridian) - the Alpine Credit Authority held its main interest rate at 1.75 percent on Monday and said it expects to keep it unchanged until at least next spring as inflation stays within its target range.

The decision was unanimous and in line with the forecast of all 22 economists polled by Meridian. The authority said it expects inflation of 0.7 percent in 2027 and 1.0 percent in 2028, both inside its target of 0 to 2 percent.

Growth projections were trimmed slightly. The authority now sees the economy expanding by 1.1 percent next year, down from 1.4 percent in its previous forecast, citing weaker export orders from neighbouring countries. The authority has now left rates unchanged at four consecutive meetings. Its main concern, it said, is the strength of the franc, which has risen about 5 percent against the euro this year and makes imports cheaper but squeezes exporters such as watchmakers and machinery makers, which employ roughly one in six workers.

"Policy is in the right place for now," a statement from the authority's board said. Board member Corinne Baumgartner told a news conference that the bank "does not see a case for cutting and does not see a case for raising".

The franc eased 0.3 percent against the euro to 0.9340 after the announcement, and government bond yields were little changed.

Mortgage lenders said the decision is good news for borrowers who fix their rates in the coming weeks. The Zurich Property Owners' Association said household budgets were still under strain from high rents. The next scheduled decision is on 15 December.

title: Danube Athletic beat Tagus United 2-1 to reach Shield Cup quarter-finals
summary: Danube Athletic came from behind to beat Tagus United 2-1 in Vienna and book a place in the Continental Shield Cup quarter-finals. Substitute Matteo Brandl scored the winner in the 84th minute.
body_html:
VIENNA, 27 October (Meridian) - Danube Athletic came from behind to beat Tagus United 2-1 on Sunday and reach the quarter-finals of the Continental Shield Cup, with substitute Matteo Brandl scoring the winner six minutes from time.

A crowd of 17,300 in Vienna saw the visitors take the lead in the 23rd minute through Diogo Salvador, who struck a low shot from the edge of the area after a quick break. Danube had 64 percent of possession in the first half but created little.

The hosts equalised in the 58th minute when captain Lukas Prinz headed in a corner from Emre Yilmaz. Brandl, on as a substitute in the 71st minute, then collected a short pass from Yilmaz and hit a left-footed shot into the far corner. The result lifts Danube to second place in its domestic league as well, a point behind the leaders. The club had been written off by many local pundits after losing its first two matches of the season, but has since won eight of its last ten, with a defence that has conceded just six goals in that run.

"We kept believing, even when we were behind," said Danube coach Josef Aigner. "The players made a difference when it counted, and the crowd carried us the last 20 minutes."

Tagus United finished the match with ten men after defender Rui Matos was sent off for a second booking in the 90th minute. Coach Paulo Veiga said he was proud of his young side but accepted that "we gave away the ball too cheaply late on".

Danube won the two-leg tie 4-3 on aggregate after a 2-2 draw in Lisbon last week. It is the club's first quarter-final in the competition in 11 years. The draw for the last eight takes place in Nyon on Thursday.

title: Tanzanian runner wins Valencia Coastal Half Marathon in course record
summary: Daudi Mwangale won the Valencia Coastal Half Marathon in a course record of 58 minutes 41 seconds. About 18,000 runners took part along the seafront.
body_html:
VALENCIA, 25 October (Meridian) - Daudi Mwangale of Tanzania won the Valencia Coastal Half Marathon on Sunday in a course record of 58 minutes 41 seconds, finishing 14 seconds clear of his nearest rival on a bright, windless morning.

The 26-year-old broke clear of a lead group of five at the 15-kilometre mark and ran the last five kilometres alone along the seafront promenade. The previous record of 59:03 had stood since 2023.

Ethiopia's Tadesse Worku took second in 58:55 and Kenya's Wilfred Rotich was third in 59:12. All three finished inside the old record. The weather was close to ideal, with temperatures of 14 degrees and almost no wind. Splits showed the leaders passed the 10-kilometre mark in 27:46, a pace that would have broken the 10,000 metres road record had it been run on a certified course, and which cost two pacemakers their legs earlier than planned.

"The pace was fast from the start and I felt strong," Mwangale said after crossing the line. "I came here to run a fast time, not just to win. Now I want to try the marathon next spring."

In the women's race, Spain's Lucia Ferrandis won in 1:07:20, a personal best by almost a minute. She was followed by Dutch runner Femke Vos, who finished in 1:07:48.

Organisers said about 18,000 runners from 71 countries took part, a record for the event, which began in 2019. Race director Pau Climent said the flat course, mild weather and a new elite pacing plan were all factors in the fast times. The race's governing body must still ratify the course record.

title: Team Alpenglow's Marit Solberg takes Tour of the Dolomites lead after stage 4
summary: Marit Solberg won the mountain stage of the Tour of the Dolomites and took the overall lead by 41 seconds. Two more mountain stages remain.
body_html:
CORTINA D'AMPEZZO, 24 October (Meridian) - Marit Solberg of Team Alpenglow won the fourth stage of the Tour of the Dolomites on Friday and took the overall lead by 41 seconds, with two mountain stages still to come.

The Norwegian attacked on the final climb to Cortina d'Ampezzo, 6 kilometres from the line, and dropped overnight leader Giulia Ferrante on a section averaging 11 percent. She finished the 142-kilometre stage in 4 hours 12 minutes 9 seconds.

Ferrante, of Team Valtellina, held on to second place overall after limiting her losses to 52 seconds. Third overall is Belgian rider Noor Peeters, 1 minute 18 seconds behind. Solberg, who finished fifth last year, said the team had planned the move for two days and that the key was patience on the lower slopes. Her team's directeur, Tomasz Wrobel, said Ferrante had been the strongest rider on the first three stages and that nobody in the team considers the race decided.

"I knew this was the day to try," Solberg said. "My legs were good and the team did a perfect job to keep me at the front until the foot of the climb."

Ferrante said she was disappointed but not discouraged. "There are still two hard days. I will try something on Sunday," she said.

Organisers said about 3,500 spectators lined the final climb in cold, cloudy weather, and the race medic reported no serious crashes, though six riders abandoned with illness or minor injuries. Stage 5 is a 168-kilometre route with three categorised climbs and finishes in Bolzano. The Tour ends on Sunday afternoon in Bolzano, where the final podium ceremony is scheduled for 17:00.

title: Hamburg Harbour Hawks sign Lithuanian guard Matas Jankus on two-year deal
summary: The Hamburg Harbour Hawks signed Lithuanian guard Matas Jankus on a two-year contract. The 24-year-old averaged 15.2 points last season.
body_html:
HAMBURG, 27 October (Meridian) - the Hamburg Harbour Hawks signed Lithuanian guard Matas Jankus on a two-year contract on Monday, the club said, adding scoring to a team that has lost three of its last five league games.

The 24-year-old arrives from Kaunas Riverside, where he averaged 15.2 points and 5.4 assists per game last season. He is expected to make his debut on Saturday against Cologne.

Club general manager Sven Petersen said the signing fills the biggest gap in the squad. "We needed a playmaker who can score under pressure, and Matas does both," he said at a news conference. The team has had a difficult start under new coach Emil Hartung, who took over in the summer after a run of poor results last season. Its offence ranks 12th in the league at 74.1 points per game, and the club hopes that Jankus's three-point shooting, at 41 percent last year, will stretch opposing defences.

Jankus said he had been following the team for years and was drawn by the club's record of developing young players. "Hamburg is a basketball city with a loud arena. I want to help us climb the table," he said.

The Hawks are eighth in the 16-team league with four wins and four defeats. They were without starting guard Jonas Kruse for the last two matches because of an ankle injury, and he is due back at the end of the month.

The club did not disclose financial terms. Local media reported a fee of about 300,000 euros to release the player from his contract. Jankus will wear number 7.

title: Two seeds fall on opening day of Tokyo Table Tennis Finals
summary: Two top-eight seeds lost on the opening day of the Tokyo Table Tennis Finals. Qualifier Hana Mizuno beat the number three seed in five games.
body_html:
TOKYO, 27 October (Meridian) - two top-eight seeds were knocked out on the opening day of the Tokyo Table Tennis Finals on Monday, including third seed Yuna Park, who lost in five games to qualifier Hana Mizuno.

Mizuno, ranked 41st, won 11-8, 9-11, 11-6, 8-11, 11-9 in front of a noisy crowd of 3,800 at the Metropolitan Gymnasium. She saved two game points in the final game.

"I told myself to be brave and keep attacking," Mizuno said. "I had nothing to lose, and the crowd lifted me." Park said she made too many errors on her backhand and congratulated her opponent. The surprise results shook up the draw. Mizuno will now meet Taiwan's Lin Shu-fen, a former finalist, in the next round, while Brazil's Duarte faces the winner of a match between two former champions, an unexpectedly open path for a 27-year-old playing the main draw for the first time in his career.

In the men's draw, sixth seed Lars Henningsen of Denmark lost 3-1 to Brazil's Caio Duarte, who hit 32 winners to the Dane's 19. The other seeds all advanced.

The finals bring together the top 16 men and top 16 women of the season. The winners will each take home 200,000 dollars from a prize pool of 1.6 million dollars.

Tournament director Kenji Aoyama said advance ticket sales were up 22 percent on last year, helped by a new free-to-air television deal. Quarter-finals begin on Wednesday. Organisers said the second day of play will feature all four remaining top-eight seeds, and that the arena will open its doors at 09:00.

title: Los Angeles orchestra announces 2027 season built around new commissions
summary: The Pacific Coast Philharmonic announced its 2027 season, with eight new commissions and a residency by Nigerian composer Folake Adeyemi-Ross. Subscriptions open next week.
body_html:
LOS ANGELES, 26 October (Meridian) - the Pacific Coast Philharmonic announced a 2027 season on Sunday built around eight new commissions, including a residency by Nigerian composer Folake Adeyemi-Ross and a youth opera written with 200 local schoolchildren.

The season, which opens on 14 January, includes 32 programmes at the orchestra's home in downtown Los Angeles. Of the 41 works scheduled, 19 were written in the last 15 years, the highest share in the orchestra's 40-year history.

Adeyemi-Ross will write a 40-minute symphonic work for choir and orchestra, based on interviews with migrants in the city. "I want audiences to hear the sound of the city in it," she said at the launch. "Not as a postcard, but as a conversation." The programme also includes a new staging of a 20th century choral classic, with a 120-voice community chorus drawn from 14 neighbourhood choirs, and a three-week series of late-night concerts of electronic and classical music, aimed at attracting audiences in their twenties, which sold out in a pilot run last spring.

Music director Tobias Reinholt said the orchestra aimed to attract younger listeners without dropping the classics. "Beethoven and Brahms are still the backbone," he said. "But a living orchestra has to play living composers."

The orchestra said it will cut the price of the cheapest tickets from 25 dollars to 15 dollars for anyone under 30 and keep 1,000 free seats for community groups. Chief executive Dana Whitlock said the plan is paid for by a 12 million dollar gift from an anonymous donor.

Subscriptions open on 3 November, and single tickets go on sale in December. The orchestra reported a 9 percent rise in subscribers this year after four years of decline. Several concerts will be streamed live.

title: Lisbon film festival gives top prize to Icelandic drama Salt Season
summary: Salt Season, a drama about a fishing family in northern Iceland, won the Golden Anchor at the Lisbon Atlantic Film Festival. The jury praised its patient storytelling and its cast of non-professional actors.
body_html:
LISBON, 25 October (Meridian) - Salt Season, a drama about a fishing family in northern Iceland, won the Golden Anchor, the top prize at the Lisbon Atlantic Film Festival, at a ceremony on Saturday night.

Directed by Birna Stefansdottir in her second feature, the film follows three generations of a family as their small harbour town loses its last fish-processing plant. Much of the cast are non-professional actors from the town where it was shot.

The jury, led by Portuguese director Ines Carvalhal, praised its "patience, humour and enormous generosity towards its characters". The prize carries 40,000 euros and a guaranteed distribution deal in Portugal. The festival's competition section included 14 films, among them eight from first or second-time directors. A special mention went to the documentary Harbour Light, about a retired lighthouse keeper in the Azores, and the audience prize was won by the family comedy Grandmother's Bicycle.

"We made this film with people who live on the same streets as the characters," Stefansdottir said as she accepted the award. "This belongs to them."

The runner-up prize went to The Orchard Road, a Moroccan-Belgian co-production directed by Yasmine Bennani, and the best actor award to Brazil's Otavio Lemos for his role in the comedy Last Tram to Santos.

The nine-day festival, now in its 12th year, drew 61,000 admissions, up from 54,000 last year, and showed 118 films from 44 countries. The festival said next year's edition will run from 16 to 25 October. Salt Season will open in Portuguese cinemas in January and is due to play at several European festivals before a limited release in the United States next spring.

title: Venice architecture show opens with focus on repairing existing buildings
summary: The Lagoon Architecture Forum opened in Venice with a main exhibition on repairing and reusing old buildings rather than building new ones. More than 60 studios from 30 countries are taking part.
body_html:
VENICE, 27 October (Meridian) - the Lagoon Architecture Forum opened in Venice on Monday with a main exhibition on repairing and reusing existing buildings, a theme its curators say reflects the carbon cost of new construction.

More than 60 architecture studios from 30 countries are showing work at the former rope factory and in the Arsenale. Exhibits include a school in Lagos extended using salvaged timber and a Rotterdam tower block whose concrete frame was kept and re-clad.

Curator Elisa Contarini said the show was a response to figures that attribute about 37 percent of global emissions from energy and processes to buildings and construction. "The greenest building is the one that already exists," she said. The forum has become one of the most closely watched events in the architecture calendar since it began 12 years ago. This year's edition is the first to run through winter, a decision the organisers took to cut crowds at the height of tourism season and to lower the costs of heating the exhibition spaces.

Not everyone was convinced. Architect Anders Rolfsen, speaking at the opening, said repair is "a fine idea, but it cannot replace new housing in cities that are growing by 3 percent a year".

Visitors can walk through a full-scale model of a repaired apartment, built with 86 percent reused material. The forum says the model will be disassembled and given to a housing cooperative at the end of the show.

The forum runs until 29 March, and the organisers expect about 280,000 visitors. Details on ticket prices are still to be confirmed.

title: Debut novelist Ilse Brandmeyer wins Frankfurt fiction prize for The Quiet Archive
summary: Ilse Brandmeyer won the Rhine Fiction Prize for her debut novel The Quiet Archive, a story set in a provincial records office. The prize is worth 25,000 euros.
body_html:
FRANKFURT, 26 October (Meridian) - Ilse Brandmeyer, a 34-year-old former librarian, won the Rhine Fiction Prize on Sunday for her debut novel The Quiet Archive, set in a provincial records office in the years after the war.

The prize, worth 25,000 euros, was announced at a ceremony in Frankfurt on the eve of the city's autumn book market. Brandmeyer beat five other finalists, two of them previous winners of national awards.

The jury chair, critic Matthias Kellner, said the novel was "a quiet book that gets louder the longer you sit with it". He praised the author's control of tone and her use of official documents as narrative. Critics have compared the novel's restrained style to the work of the late 20th century writers who wrote about bureaucracy and memory. Brandmeyer, who still works part-time at a municipal library near Cologne, said she wrote most of it on early morning train journeys and does not yet plan to leave the job.

"I spent six years working with old files," Brandmeyer said. "I kept thinking about the people behind every form, who never imagined anyone would read them."

The book was first printed in an edition of only 3,000 copies by the independent publisher Linden Press. The publisher said it has ordered a reprint of 25,000 and that translation rights have been sold in nine countries.

The other finalists included Marco Zanetti for Winter Tenants and Selin Aydin for Ferry Hour. The author's next book is due in 2028. The Quiet Archive has sold more than 40,000 copies since publication in March, a strong figure for a literary debut in a market where most first novels sell fewer than 2,000.

title: Amsterdam museum to return 18 sculptures to heritage authority in Benin City
summary: The Canal House Museum in Amsterdam will return 18 sculptures to a heritage authority in Benin City after a review of how they were acquired. The objects will leave in the spring.
body_html:
AMSTERDAM, 26 October (Meridian) - the Canal House Museum in Amsterdam said on Monday it will return 18 sculptures to a heritage authority in Benin City, after a two-year review concluded they were taken without consent in the 19th century.

The objects, mostly carved wood and cast brass, have been in the museum's collection since 1912. They will be shipped in the spring after conservation and a joint catalogue, the museum said.

"The review left no reasonable doubt about how these objects reached us," museum director Femke Hartog told reporters. "Returning them is the right thing to do and it is long overdue." The decision follows a growing number of similar returns by European museums in recent years. The Dutch government has said it supports restitution of objects taken in colonial contexts, and the museum's board said it will now review another 60 objects of uncertain origin in its Africa collection.

The Edo Heritage Commission, which will receive the works, welcomed the decision. Its representative, Osagie Ehigiator, said the sculptures would go on public display in a new museum building in Benin City, due to open in 2028.

The two institutions will keep working together. The Amsterdam museum will lend replicas for an exhibition on the shared history of the objects, and three curators from Benin City will spend a year at the museum.

The museum said the cost of the return, estimated at 1.3 million euros, will be paid from its own funds and from a Dutch government grant for provenance research. A panel of external experts reviewed the findings.
